claims.text: Equal-atomic NbMoTaW forms a single-phase BCC solid solution.
Conventionally processed NbMoTaW has coarse grains on the order of tens of micrometers.
Equal-atomic NbMoTaW has intrinsically poor room-temperature ductility.
Untreated NbMoTaW has excellent mechanical strength at 1600 °C.
NbMoTaW has irradiation resistance predicted by first-principles calculations.
HPT at approximately 2.5 GPa for 15 revolutions will refine NbMoTaW into a uniform submicron-grained structure.
HPT grain refinement will increase the grain-boundary density in NbMoTaW.
The increased grain-boundary density will facilitate dislocation nucleation, emission, mobility, and absorption.
Grain-boundary-assisted local plasticity will transform room-temperature behavior from brittle to more ductile.
HPT processing will retain the single-phase BCC lattice without detrimental phase changes.
Retention of the BCC lattice will preserve NbMoTaW's high-temperature strength at 1600 °C.
The added grain boundaries will act as sinks where irradiation-induced defects recombine.
Defect recombination at grain boundaries will preserve the irradiation resistance of HPT-processed NbMoTaW.
HPT-processed NbMoTaW will have a markedly higher room-temperature fracture strain than untreated NbMoTaW.
HPT-processed NbMoTaW will maintain yield and fracture strengths at 1600 °C similar to the untreated alloy.
HPT-processed NbMoTaW will retain irradiation resistance comparable to the untreated alloy.
The proposed benefits require the submicron grain structure to remain stable during exposure at 1600 °C.
Contamination, secondary phases, or excessive HPT-induced residual stresses could negate the ductility, high-temperature, or irradiation benefits.
